The economic landscape shifted from manufacturing to service industries, concentrating wealth in urban cores while widening the gap between high and low earners.

*   **Industrial Shift:** Manufacturing jobs peaked at 19.5 million in 1979 but fell to under 11.5 million during the pandemic (approx. 2020–2023 period referenced) [Source: ev-8] [Source: ev-11]. Conversely, employment in finance and professional/business services soared from 12 million to 32 million [Source: ev-8] [Source: ev-11]. Housing costs have outpaced wage growth significantly since 2000.

*   **Price-to-Income Gap:** Since 2000, median household income in the U.S. grew by 92% (from $41,990 to $80,610), while median home prices nearly tripled, jumping 177% from $122,775 to $339,937 [Source: ev-6] [Source: ev-11]. Other major cities like New York City, Miami, and Boston also face significant pressures where home prices far outpace local incomes [Source: ev-6]. The Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024 representing a 225% increase since January 2000 [Source: ev-11].

Gentrification has led to displacement that disproportionately affects minority communities due to structural housing market constraints.

*   **Racial Demographics:** Urban areas have become less white; the share of non-Hispanic whites fell by 7 points in urban cores and 8 points in suburbs since 2000 [Source: ev-7] [Source: ev-11]. In summary, from 1980 to 2024, American cities experienced a fundamental transformation where service-industry growth fueled gentrification in major metro cores.
